## Levels, Precision, and Time

As stated in the introduction, numbers get worse in three ways as we compute on them: noise, level, and time.

In this table,

- **precision** refers to a way an encryption of a number "decays with time" (as all known fully homomorphic schemes do). The basic idea is that after an operation, the new reseult will have some added mathematical noise.

  - For example, adding $Enc(r_*)$ and $Enc(s_*)$ to get $Enc(t_*)$, $t_i=r_i+s_i+e_i$ for some error $e_i$, so it is good to always assume our numbers are possibly off by some "noise" which accumulates as more operations are done on them.

  - This shouldn't be too surprising (e.g. in Python, 0.1 + 0.3 is not exactly 0.4).

  - As a default, we assume starting noise (lack of precision) is around $10^{-10}$.

- **(encryption) level** refers to the decryptability.

  - For example, assume a fresh ciphertext starts off at "level 35."
  - Multiplying two "level 30" numbers give "level 29" numbers, and level 0 numbers should be considered decryptable by a reasonable adversary and should be avoided.

- **time** is self-explanatory, but remember we are doing very parallelizable computation for the sake of applications.

|     | + | x | conjugation / cycles | 
| ------ | --------- | -------- | -------- | 
| time | $50 \mu s$     | $4 ms$ (proportional to level)     | $4 ms$    |
| precision | noises add     | noises stay constant     | constant $10^{-10}$ worse    |
| level | $a,b \rightarrow min(a,b)$     | $a,b \rightarrow \min(a,b) -1$     | id     | 

Therefore, as we build additional functions, we must keep in mind the cost of each individual function, since each auxiliary function builds into more complex functions.

:::{.callout-tip icon=false title="**Remark**"}

1. In the rest of the book, for the sake of simplicity, we will be optimizing for the amount of "operations", which is proportional to the costs we have in the table.

2. In section III and IV, you are thrown into the proverbial deep end as you will see costs skyrocket.

:::
